i: This Book takes its name from the writer, who was cupbearer to Artaxerxes (surnamed Longimanus) king of Persia, and was sent by him with a commission to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem. It is also called the second book of Ezra; because it is a continuation of the history, begun by Ezra, of the state of the people of God after their return from captivity.

a.1: Nehemiah hearing the miserable state of his countrymen in Judea, laments, fasts, and prays to God for their relief.
a.2: Nehemiah with commission from king Artaxerxes comes to Jerusalem: and exhorts the Jews to rebuild the walls.
a.3: They begin to build the walls: the names and order of the builders.
a.4: The building is carried on notwithstanding the opposition of their enemies.
a.5: Nehemiah blames the rich, for their oppressing the poor. His exhortation, and bounty to his countrymen.
a.6: The enemies seek to terrify Nehemiah. He proceeds and finishes the wall.
a.7: Nehemiah appoints watchmen in Jerusalem. The list of those who came first from Babylon.
a.8: Ezra reads the law before the people. Nehemiah comforts them. They celebrate the feast of tabernacles.
a.9: The people repent with fasting and sackcloth. The Levites confess God's benefits, and the people's ingratitude: they pray for them, and make a covenant with God.
a.10: The names of the subscribers to the covenant, and the contents of it.
a.11: Who were the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and the other cities.
a.12: The priests, and Levites that came up with Zerubbabel. The succession of high priests: the solemnity of the dedication of the wall.

7:69: (Hitherto is related what was written in the record. From this place forward goes on the history of Nehemiah.)
7:70: Athersatha... That is, Nehemiah; as appears from chap. 12. Either that he was so called at the court of the king of Persia, where he was cupbearer: or that, as some think, this name signifies governor; and he was at that time governor of Judea.
9:7: The fire of the Chaldeans... The city of Ur in Chaldea, the name of which signifies fire. Or out of the fire of the tribulations and temptations, to which he was there exposed.-The ancient Rabbins understood this literally, affirming that Abram was cast into the fire by the idolaters, and brought out by a miracle without any hurt.
9:17: And gave the head... That is, they set their head, or were bent to return to Egypt.
12:46: Sanctified... That is, they gave them that which by the law was set aside, and sanctified for their use.
13:4: Over this thing, etc... Or, he was faulty in this thing, or in this kind.
